subject: Accounting
title: Make or Buy Decisions
description: A quick, practical guide to Make or Buy Decisions.

hook.text: Should a car company make its own seats or buy them from a supplier? The numbers decide.

buildup.text: Make-or-buy analysis compares the full cost of in-house production against purchasing externally.

discovery.text: Include materials, labor, overhead, quality control—and the opportunity cost of using that capacity.

twist.text: Buying might be cheaper, but outsourcing risks quality issues and supply chain dependency.

climax.text: The best decisions weigh both the numbers and the strategic implications of each option.

punchline.text: Cheaper isn't always better. Cost is only part of the answer.

quiz.question: What does make-or-buy analysis compare?
options: In-house production cost vs. external purchase cost

details.summary: Make-or-buy decisions evaluate whether a company should produce a component internally or purchase it from an external supplier. This topic covers the quantitative cost comparison and qualitative factors like quality control, capacity, and strategic risk.
details.whyItMatters: Outsourcing the wrong component can create supply chain vulnerability, while insourcing everything wastes resources on non-core activities. Proper analysis reveals the best option.
takeaways: Compare only relevant costs: the avoidable costs of making versus the purchase price from buying
Opportunity cost of using limited capacity internally may tip the decision toward buying
Qualitative factors like quality control, reliability, and proprietary knowledge often outweigh cost differences

faq.question: How do you analyze a make-or-buy decision?
faq.answer: List all costs of making the component (direct materials, labor, variable overhead, and any avoidable fixed costs) and compare to the purchase price plus any additional costs of buying (shipping, quality inspection). Include opportunity cost of capacity used.

faq.question: What qualitative factors affect make-or-buy decisions?
faq.answer: Key qualitative factors include quality control (easier in-house), supply reliability (risk of supplier failure), capacity availability, intellectual property protection, supplier relationship management, and whether the component is core to the company's competency.
